Create an interactive Kaplan-Meier survival curve

Source: R/survivalCurve.R
survivalCurve.Rd

Fits a Kaplan-Meier survival curve with survival::survfit() and draws it as an interactive plotly figure. The curves and their confidence bands are drawn by VizModules::linePlot() from the curve's step coordinates, so the band takes its line's colour, sits underneath it and toggles with it from the legend.

Usage

survivalCurve(
  data,
  time,
  status,
  group.by = NULL,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  conf.type = c("log", "log-log", "plain"),
  conf.int.opacity = 0.25,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = FALSE,
  censor = TRUE,
  surv.median.line = "none",
  fun = NULL,
  palette.selection = NULL,
  line.size = 2,
  break.time.by = NULL,
  legend.title = NULL,
  pairwise = FALSE,
  pairs = NULL,
  p.adjust.method = "holm"
)

Arguments

data

A data frame containing at least the time and status columns.

time

The name of the numeric follow-up time column.

status

The name of the event/status indicator column.

group.by

Optional name of a categorical column to stratify the curves by. When NULL or "" a single overall survival curve (named "All") is drawn.

conf.int

Logical; draw a confidence band around each curve (default TRUE).

conf.level

Confidence level of the band, between 0 and 1 (default 0.95), passed to survival::survfit() as its conf.int.

conf.type

How the band is computed, one of "log" (the survival::survfit() default), "log-log" or "plain".

conf.int.opacity

Fill opacity of the band, between 0 and 1 (default 0.25).

pval

Logical; display the log-rank test p-value. Only applied when group.by defines more than one group (default TRUE).

risk.table

Logical; append a "number at risk" table beneath the curve (default FALSE). The table has no gridlines; its time axis zooms with the curve's.

censor

Logical; draw censoring marks (default TRUE).

surv.median.line

Character; draw median survival reference lines. One of "none", "hv", "h", or "v" (default "none"). Drawn only for the survival probability and percentage curves.

fun

Optional transformation of the survival curve. One of NULL or "survival" (survival probability), "pct" (survival percentage), "event" (cumulative events, 1 - S), or "cumhaz" (cumulative hazard, -log(S)). The band is transformed with the curve.

palette.selection

Optional vector of colors for the strata, named by stratum level (an unnamed vector is used in level order).

line.size

Numeric width of the survival curves in pixels (default 2).

break.time.by

Optional numeric spacing between x-axis tick marks, which also sets the times the risk table counts at.

legend.title

Legend title. Defaults to group.by when stratified.

pairwise

Logical; also test each pair of groups (default FALSE). Only applied when group.by defines three or more groups; with two, the pairwise test is the global one. See Details for how to read the results.

pairs

Optional list of length-2 character vectors naming the pairs to test, e.g. list(c("Asymptomatic", "Symptomatic")), as for VizModules::compute_pairwise_stats(). NULL (the default) tests every pair. The p-values are adjusted across the pairs tested.

p.adjust.method

A stats::p.adjust() method for the pairwise p-values (default "holm").

Value

A plotly::plot_ly() object containing the interactive survival curve, with a per-stratum summary (subjects, events, median survival and its confidence interval, and the log-rank test) as attribute "table". With pairwise, attribute "pairwise" holds a row per comparison: group1, group2, their subjects (n1, n2) and events (events1, events2), the log-rank chisq and p.value, the adjusted p.adj and its p.adjust.method, and the hazard ratio of group2 relative to group1 (hr) with its 95% confidence interval (hr.lower, hr.upper), NA when a group has no events or the model has no finite estimate.

Details

The input data should be in the "tidy" survival format: one row per subject with a numeric follow-up time column and a status (event) indicator. The status column may be numeric (0/1 where 1 = event, or 1/2 where 2 = event, following the survival::Surv() conventions), logical (TRUE = event), or a two-level factor/character where the level containing "dead"/"death"/"event"/"yes"/"true"/"1" is treated as the event.

When group.by is supplied the curve is stratified by that column and the log-rank test p-value (from survival::survdiff()) can be shown via pval.

Comparing three or more groups. The log-rank test above is a global test: it asks whether survival differs anywhere among the groups, not which groups differ. With pairwise = TRUE and three or more groups, each pair is also tested on its own subjects (a log-rank test of the two groups, as survminer's pairwise_survdiff() computes), and the results are listed on the plot and returned as attribute "pairwise". To read them:

  • The p-values are adjusted for the number of comparisons made (p.adjust.method, default Holm, which keeps the chance of any false positive among them at the nominal level; "BH" controls the false discovery rate instead and suits screening many groups; "none" overstates significance). Testing only the comparisons that matter (pairs, each group against a control, say) costs less power. The adjustment covers only the comparisons in this call: picking them after looking at the curves, or regrouping the data until something is significant, is not accounted for.

  • A p-value does not say how large a difference is. Each pair also gets the hazard ratio (hr) of group2 relative to group1, from a Cox model of the pair, with its 95% confidence interval: above 1, group2 has the higher hazard (shorter survival). The interval is not adjusted for multiplicity, and being a Wald interval it can disagree slightly with the log-rank p-value near the significance cut-off.

  • The log-rank test is most sensitive when one group's hazard is a constant multiple of the other's (proportional hazards). Curves that cross can hide a real difference, and the hazard ratio then averages over opposite effects, so read the tests against the curves.

  • Groups with few subjects or events give unstable results; in survival_lung, ph.ecog's "In bed >50%" group is a single subject, yet its comparisons come out "significant". Check n1, n2, events1 and events2, and drop or merge sparse groups before testing.

  • The tests ignore any order among the groups (stage, dose), for which a trend test is more powerful, and they are unadjusted for other covariates: see forestPlot() for a Cox model with covariates.

The figure is built natively in plotly rather than converted from a ggplot: plotly::ggplotly() cannot draw the stepped confidence band survminer uses.

See also

survival::survfit(), VizModules::linePlot(), survivalCurveInputsUI(), survivalCurveServer(), survivalCurveApp()

Author

Jacob Martin, Jared Andrews

Examples

library(sciVizModules)
data(survival_lung)
fig <- survivalCurve(survival_lung,
    time = "time", status = "status", group.by = "sex"
)
if (interactive()) fig

# Cumulative events with a number-at-risk table.
fig2 <- survivalCurve(survival_lung,
    time = "time", status = "status", group.by = "sex",
    fun = "event", risk.table = TRUE
)

# Four performance-status groups, each pair compared.
fig3 <- survivalCurve(survival_lung,
    time = "time", status = "status", group.by = "ph.ecog", pairwise = TRUE
)
attr(fig3, "pairwise")
